newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Trial rakes up E.Berlin's murky terror links.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Trial rakes up E.Berlin's murky terror links.

text.p: Even the West German investigators who rubbed their hands in gleeful anticipation of the Cold War secrets the fall of the Berlin Wall would reveal could hardly have expected to find a handful of most wanted urban guerrillas lurking in its shadow.

In the summer of 1990, 10 members of the Red Army Faction (RAF), the leftist gang that terrorised the West German establishment in the 1970s and 1980s, were arrested after hiding in East Germany for nearly a decade.

Under new identities, they had been living as ordinary East German citizens, working and bringing up families in the former Soviet satellite. Three of them were regarded as being among West Germany's most dangerous criminals.
For many, the question was: What did the rulers of a stagnant Communist administration have in common with the proponents of armed revolutionary struggle?

On February 19, four former East German security officers who helped the guerrillas recast themselves in East German society go on trial in Berlin on charges of preventing the West German authorities bringing the fugitives to justice.

It is one of a series of cases aimed at establishing the extent to which East Berlin supported international terrorism and punishing those behind the "unholy alliance" of the RAF and the hated Ministry for State Security (Stasi).
DIFFICULTY IN PROVING STASI TERROR LINK
Investigators tried initially to nail former Stasi officers for aiding and abetting two RAF attacks in West Germany.

Arrest warrants were issued for ex-Stasi chief Erich Mielke and several top officers on charges of being accomplices in the attempted murder of U.S. General Frederik Kroesen in Heidelberg and military personnel at the U.S. airbase at Ramstein.

But, although RAF guerrillas disclosed how East German commandos taught them to use weapons and explosives, prosecutors could not prove this had been before the two 1981 attacks and therefore contributed to them.

Prosecutors only once succeeded in proving the Stasi's active support for guerrillas, when ex-Stasi colonel Helmut Voigt was convicted in 1994 of helping guerrilla mastermind "Carlos the Jackal" carry out a fatal bomb attack on the French cultural centre in West Berlin in 1983.
The officers due to go on trial on Wednesday, like their colleague Voigt who was jailed for four years, were top cadres at the Stasi's counter-terrorist department.
The department was set up after a Palestinian guerrilla attack at the 1972 Olympic Games in Munich to gather information and head off potential attacks at home.
TERROR LINKS DESPITE PUBLIC CONDEMNATION
Publicly East Berlin condemned terrorism.

But secretly it supported guerrilla warfare -- as long as it was aimed at its Cold War enemies -- providing escape routes, hideouts, travel papers and turning a blind eye to the smuggling of arms and explosives in and out of the country.

"Mielke was notoriously scared of terrorism and obsessed with finding out as much as possible about guerrillas in West Germany to prevent attacks in East Germany," said Fritz Schmaldienst, the co-author of a book about Johannes Weinrich, Carlos's German deputy.

"He forged links with terrorists because that was the price to pay to gain insight into their methods and plans," said Schmaldienst, who based his book on Hungarian sources close to the Carlos gang and interviews with ex-Stasi officers.
East Berlin was just one of many East bloc havens for guerrillas, who fled the scene of their bloody deeds via eastern Europe to commando training camps and bases in the Middle East.
"It was Moscow's policy to help the Palestinian liberation movement, this extended to groups that split off from Yasser Arafat," Schmaldienst said.
"So when Carlos joined forces with the Palestinians, the Soviet satellites were expected to help him too."

Carlos was barred from entering East Germany in 1980 after cavorting indiscreetly in East Berlin night clubs and bars as he passed through the capital on his terror assignments. The Stasi feared he might be spotted by foreign agents.
MOTIVES FOR TERROR LINK STILL NOT CLEAR
The Stasi's murky links with terrorists continued right up to the end of the Cold War, but German experts are still divided over what was really behind the "unholy alliance".
They shared a common enemy -- the United States and its Western allies -- and a common ideological aim in their fight against capitalism and "international imperialism".

Experts agree the links helped them to gather information and prevent attacks at home, but they are still unsure whether the aim was also to destabilise the West -- something former East German rulers have vehemently denied.
Lawyers defending the four ex-Stasi officers argue that their clients did a good deed taking 10 guerrillas out of circulation and turning them into harmless, law-abiding citizens.

"They didn't help them because they approved of their crimes. Once the terrorists moved to East Germany they were kept under strict surveillance and forbidden to have any contact with their former comrades," said lawyer Manfred Studier of the successors to the notorious Baader-Meinhof gang.
"They dropped out of the terrorist scene and renounced violence. There was no risk they'd carry out more attacks."

Since the end of the Cold War, several major guerrilla attacks during the last three decades have been traced back to East Berlin. It has yet to be established whether the authorities turned a blind eye to certain embassies' involvement or actively participated.

This month five people, two of them employees at East Berlin's former Libyan embassy, were charged with carrying out a 1986 bomb attack at a West Berlin disco that killed two off-duty U.S. soldiers and a Turkish woman. The attack, ordered by Libya, prompted U.S. bombing raids on Tripoli.
Given the Stasi's obsession with collecting information about guerrillas, experts argue they must at least have known about such attacks in advance, Schmaldienst said.

"There was a huge Stasi presence at the 1972 Munich Olympic Games. Perhaps they knew about the (Palestinian) attack in advance," said Schmaldienst. "But there is no proof and no one would admit if it were true."
The Stasi's anti-terrorist methods were unconventional but achieved their goal. No guerrilla attack was ever carried out against the country or any of its citizens.
Ironically, the masses of information they gathered have helped to nail terrorists such as Carlos now jailed and awaiting trial in Paris and Weinrich, who is to be tried in Berlin.
